'''Hans Kronberger''' [[Order of the British Empire|CBE]], [[Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="Rotheram"/> (28 July 1920 – 29 September 1970) was a British physicist. During his career with the [[UK Atomic Energy Authority]] he made important contributions to the development of the British [[thermonuclear bomb]] and nuclear power engineering, especially in the field of [[isotope separation]].

==Early life==
Hans Kronberger was born of Jewish parents in [[Linz]], Austria, where his father was a leather merchant.<ref name = "Rotheram"/> Kronberger attended the Akademische Gymnasium in Linz, matriculating in Mathematics, Latin, Greek and German; he was a brilliant scholar.<ref>
{{Cite web
| url = http://www.ooegeschichte.at/Historische_Bibliografie.64+M5306de18f3c.0.html <!-- required -->
| title = Bibliografie zur oberösterreichischen Geschichte <!-- required -->
| access-date = 5 July 2013
}}</ref> 
After the [[Anschluss]], the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in 1938, Kronberger fled to Britain, arriving at Victoria Station with £10 and his school reports. He set about gaining entry to a university and was accepted at [[Newcastle University|King's College, Newcastle]], then a college of [[Durham University]] to read mechanical engineering.<ref>
{{Citation
 | title = Dr Hans Kronberger. Distinguished nuclear physicist
 | newspaper = The Times
 | pages = 14
 | date = 1 October 1970
}}</ref> 
Following the [[Battle of France|fall of France]], in May 1940 Kronberger was classified as a "friendly enemy alien" and interned on the Isle of Man.<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Gillman <!-- author name -->
 | first = Peter
 | author-link = Peter Gillman
 | year = 1980
 | title = Collar the Lot! How Britain Interned and Expelled its Wartime Refugees <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Quartet Books
 | location = London
 | isbn = 978-0704334083 
}}</ref> 
In July 1940, Kronberger, along with some 2500 refugees, was deported to Australia on board [[HMT Dunera]]; during the voyage he and others were subjected to ill treatment.<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Bartrop <!-- author name -->
 | first = Paul R.
 | author-link = Paul R. Bartrop
 | last2 = Eisen
 | first2 = G.
 | year = 1990
 | title = The Dunera Affair: A Documentary Resource Book <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Schwartz & Wilkinson
 | location = Melbourne
 | id = .
 | page = 155
| isbn = 1863370250
 }}</ref> 
In Australia, he was interned first at a camp in [[Hay Internment and POW camps|Hay]], New South Wales, then from May 1941 at [[Tatura]] in Victoria.<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Patkin <!-- author name -->
 | first = B.
 | year = 1979
 | title = The Dunera Internees <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Cassell
 | location = Australia
 | isbn = 072696803X
 | page = 107
}}</ref> 
He was released and returned to Britain in 1942. He was tutored by refugee scientists at the camps<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Pearl <!-- author name -->
 | first = C.
 | year = 1983
 | title = The Dunera Scandal: Deported by Mistake <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Angus & Robertson
 | location = London and Sydney
 | isbn = 0207147078
 | page = 81
}}</ref> 
and it was mainly due to this experience that he changed his course to physics on resuming his studies at Newcastle. He graduated in 1944 with the Stroud Prize in Physics.<ref name = "Rotheram"/>

==Career==
In 1944 he moved to [[Birmingham University]], joining [[Francis Simon| Francis Simon's]] team in the [[Tube Alloys]] Project, the British programme to develop an atomic bomb.<ref>
{{Cite ODNB
 | last = Penney
 | first = William
 | author-link = William Penney, Baron Penney
 | publisher = OUP
 | series = Oxford Dictionary of National Biography
 | chapter = Kronberger, Hans
 | chapter-url = http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/printable/34364
 | doi = 10.1093/ref:odnb/34364
| title = The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography
 | year = 2004
 }}</ref> 
His PhD on isotope separation was completed in 1948.<ref>
{{cite journal
 | last = Kronberger
 | first = H.
 | title = Partial separation of uranium isotopes by thermal diffusion of liquid uranium hexafluoride 
 | publisher = PhD Thesis
 | location = University of Birmingham
 | year = 1948
}}</ref> He then moved to the newly formed [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] at Harwell, where he continued to work on the separation of the [[isotopes of uranium]], initially by [[gaseous diffusion]] and then using high speed [[Uranium centrifuge|centrifuges]]. In 1951 he moved to [[Capenhurst]], where a large scale diffusion plant was being constructed. In two years, he was promoted to head of the Capenhurst laboratories, and then in 1958 he succeeded [[Leonard Rotherham]] as director of research and development of the industrial group of the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]].<ref name = "Rotheram"/>

In 1952, Britain committed itself to the development of a [[thermonuclear weapon]].<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Arnold <!-- author name -->
 | first = Lorna
 | author-link = Lorna Arnold
 | year = 2001
 | title = Britain and the H-Bomb <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Palgrave
 | location = Basingstoke
 | isbn = 0333947428
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1970-10-01|title=Dr. Hans Kronberger, 50; Led Nuclear Plant in Britain|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/10/01/archives/dr-hans-kronberger-50-led-nuclear-plant-in-britain.html|access-date=2020-06-30|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Kronberger's work on the separation of [[Isotopes of lithium|lithium isotopes]] was essential to the construction of the [[Operation Grapple|first warheads]], which were tested at [[Kiritimati|Christmas Island]] in 1957.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = McIntyre
 | first = Donald
 | title = Project Crystal: Lithium 6 for Thermonuclear Weapons
 | journal = UK Nuclear History
 | issue = Working Paper 5
 | publisher = Mountbatten Centre for International Studies
 | location = Southampton
 | year = 2009
 | url = http://dspace.cigilibrary.org/jspui/handle/123456789/11667
 | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130730094932/http://dspace.cigilibrary.org/jspui/handle/123456789/11667
 | url-status = dead
 | archive-date = 30 July 2013
 | access-date = 4 July 2013
 }}</ref> A series of promotions within the UKAEA followed; he became Scientist in Chief of the Reactor Group in 1962 and the Member for Reactor Development of the UKAEA in 1969.  Some of his work remains classified to this day, but there are many tributes to his inspiring leadership.<ref name = "Rotheram"/> He became involved with the promotion of peaceful uses of atomic energy and was a member of the Scientific Advisory Committee of the [[International Atomic Energy Agency]].<ref>{{Cite book
 | title = Yearbook of the United Nations 1969 <!-- required -->
 | location = New York
 | chapter = Part Two, Chapter 1, The International Atomic Energy Agency
 | chapter-url = http://unyearbook.un.org/1969YUN/1969_P2_CH1.pdf
 | access-date = 4 July 2013
 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He contributed to feasibility studies on desalination of sea water and lectured on [[hydrostatic extrusion]].<ref>
{{cite news
 | title = Making the Sea Safe to Drink
 | newspaper =The Guardian
 | pages = 5
 | date = 7 September 1966
}}</ref><ref>
{{Cite journal
 | first = Hans
 | last = Kronberger
 | year = 1969
 | title = Hydrostatic extrusion <!-- required -->
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]]
 | volume = 311
 | issue = 1506
 | pages = 331–347
 | doi=10.1098/rspa.1969.0121
|bibcode = 1969RSPSA.311..331K
 | jstor=2416236| s2cid = 110115662
 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
The Jewish population of Linz was expelled in July 1938.<ref>
{{Cite web
| url = http://www.linz.at/english/history/653.asp<!-- required -->
| title = Expulsion of the Jews <!-- required -->
| access-date = 4 July 2013
}}</ref>
Kronberger's mother was killed at [[Hartheim Euthanasia Centre|Schloss Hartheim]] and his sister was gassed at [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]].
His father survived imprisonment in the concentration camp at [[Theresienstadt concentration camp|Theresienstadt]].<ref>
{{Cite book
 | last = Schneider <!-- author name -->
 | first = G.
 | year = 1995
 | title = Exile and Destruction: The Fate of Austrian Jews, 1938–1945 <!-- required -->
 | publisher = Praeger
 | location = Westport
 | isbn = 0275951391
 | page = 186
}}</ref> 
Kronberger became a naturalised British citizen in 1946.<ref>
{{cite web
 | title = Certificate AZ18115, 14 May 1946.
 | url = http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/SearchUI/Details?uri=C11816506
 | access-date = 29 July 2013 
}}</ref> 
In 1951 he married Joan Hanson, a scientific assistant at Harwell, a widow with a young son, Paul; together they had two daughters, Zoë and Sarah. Joan was diagnosed with a brain tumour in 1952 and died in 1962. Kronberger was a talented pianist, and also a skilled mountaineer and skier.<ref name = "Rotheram"/>
